newsitem.title: USA: Astronomer, author Carl Sagan dies at 62.
newsitem.headline: Astronomer, author Carl Sagan dies at 62.

text.p: Astronomer and Pulitzer Prize-winning author Carl Sagan, who popularised science through books and television and tirelessly championed the search for life in outer space, died on Friday at age 62, hospital officials said.
Sagan died from pneumonia after a two-year battle with a rare blood disorder that led to cancer, said Susan Edmonds, spokeswoman for the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Centre.

"Through his writings and television productions, he brought the excitement and challenges of scientific discovery into the homes of millions of families here and abroad," said Hunter Rawlings, president of Cornell University, where Sagan was a professor for nearly 30 years. "We will sorely miss him."

Sagan was the author of more than 20 books and hundreds of scientific and popular articles but was best known for his 1980 television series on the workings of the universe, "Cosmos," which became the most popular in the history of public television, ultimately viewed by some 500 million people.

"No one has ever succeeded in conveying the wonders, excitement and joy of science as widely as Carl Sagan," said the National Academy of Sciences on giving him his highest honour in 1994. "His ability to capture the imagination of so many and to explain difficult concepts in understandable terms is a magnificent achievement."

Sagan held a passionate conviction that life is abundant throughout the universe and spent much of his career trying to prove it, aiming radar telescopes at distant galaxies and listening for radio signals from far-off civilisations.
"I'd rather there be extraterrestrial life discovered in my lifetime than not," he told the Washington Post recently. "I'd hate to die and never know."
Early in his career he was so convinced of the possibility of life on other planets that he argued the Viking Mars space probe should have edible paint and a flashlight to attract Martians.
Sagan was born in Brooklyn in 1934, the son of a Ukrainian immigrant garment worker and Austro-Hungarian mother.
He discovered astronomy early in life through the New York Public Library and by the age of 26 he had a Doctor of Philosophy degree in astrophysics from the University of Chicago.
Early in his career he began a long association with the space agency NASA that included a leading role in the Mariner, Viking, Voyager and Galileo expeditions.

Sagan and a Cornell colleague were responsible for the famous plaques installed on the explorer ships Pioneer 10 and 11 as calling cards to other civilisations that included a depiction of Earth's location in the Milky Way galaxy and illustrations of a nude man and woman.
In the early 1970s he began the first of many appearances on "The Tonight Show" with Johnny Carson that introduced millions to the wonders of astronomy and concepts about the origins of the universe.
Sagan has been called "an intellectual gadfly" and was sometimes belittled by fellow-scientists who said his work was too much style and not enough substance.
But Sagan never apologised for his popular work.
"Here's science dependent as never before on public funds, and so continuing science depends on public support," he once said. "And how's the public going to support it if they don't understand it?"

Sagan was the author of 20 books including "Dragons of Eden," an exploration of human intelligence that won the Pulitzer Prize in 1978, and "Cosmos" a companion to the television series that is the most widely read science book in the English language and "Broca's Brain."

Even while ill he continued working productively and completed this year's "The Demon-Haunted World," a polemic against pseudo-science. A book of essays due out next year will be titled "Billions and Billions" after Sagan's trademark phrase on the enormity of the universe.
He also wrote a novel, "Contact," which is being made into a movie starring Jodie Foster.

Sagan came to Seattle in 1995 for a bone marrow transplant to combat myelodysplasia, a rare blood disorder that leads to leukaemia. He returned to Seattle for chemotherapy this year and thought he had conquered the disease, but his condition deteriorated.
He is survived by his third wife, Ann Druyan, and five children.
